title: Incomplete and Corrupted ZIP Prevention: Tenant-Safe Multipart Export Upload Retry Gates
author: MordecaiNilsson7582
summary: A large B2B SaaS export should use multipart upload only when its size justifies the extra state. The decision rule is stricter than "all parts returned success": keep the export private, complete the multipart upload, verify the final object with HEAD, and only then expose a tenant-scoped download link. If archive generation fails, abort that upload before retrying. TL;DR: A ZIP that downloads but will not open often points to an upload that never reached a valid completed state, or to stale multipart state being reused. Treat completion as a commit. Record the upload ID and part results, abort failed jobs, and make HEAD verification the gate between uploading and ready . The byte path should bypass the application. A worker creates the private multipart session, the browser or worker sends parts to presigned destinations, and object storage assembles them. Your app carries control data, not a multi-gigabyte archive. Tenant isolation stays in that control plane: derive the bucket and key from authenticated tenant context, never accept either as free-form client authority, and issue short-lived signed access only after verification. How can an incomplete multipart export upload corrupt a ZIP download? Yes. Individual part success does not prove that the final object exists in completed form. Completion can be missing, a retry can refer to an earlier upload ID, or the application can publish a link while the job is between its last part and the complete call. A ZIP exposes the mistake because its central directory is near the end; a truncated object may download normally and fail only when opened. Use explicit states: generating , uploading , completing , verifying , ready , and failed . Only ready may trigger a customer notification. The database row should bind tenant_id , export ID, bucket, object key, and multipart upload ID. A retry gets a new attempt record or resumes the exact recorded attempt. It must never guess from a prefix. One boundary matters. If generation or any part upload fails, move the job to failed and explicitly abort its multipart session. No automatic cleanup rule for multipart fragments is assumed here, and the one-day lifecycle floor is not a substitute for immediate cleanup. This prevents abandoned parts from confusing the next attempt. Stop there. Put verification in front of notification This Python program is a publication gate for an Infrai-backed export. The base URL comes from deployment configuration so an unlinked comparison doesn't embed a vendor destination. It verifies the completed private object with HEAD and surfaces rate limits for queue-level retry. import argparse import json import os from urllib.parse import quote import requests def verify_completed_object ( bucket : str , key : str ) -> dict : base_url = os . environ [ " INFRAI_BASE_URL " ]. rstrip ( " / " ) api_key = os . environ [ " INFRAI_API_KEY " ] path = " /storage/object/head/{bucket}/{key} " . format ( bucket = quote ( bucket , safe = "" ), key = quote ( key , safe = "" ), ) response = requests . request ( method = " GET " , url = f " { base_url }{ path } " , headers = { " Authorization " : f " Bearer { api_key } " }, timeout = 30 , ) if response . status_code == 429 : delay = response . headers . get ( " Retry-After " , " unknown " ) raise RuntimeError ( f " rate limited; retry after { delay } seconds " ) if not response . ok : raise RuntimeError ( f " HEAD failed ( { response . status_code } ): { response . text } " ) return response . json () parser = argparse . ArgumentParser () parser . add_argument ( " --bucket " , required = True ) parser . add_argument ( " --key " , required = True ) args = parser . parse_args () print ( json . dumps ( verify_completed_object ( args . bucket , args . key ), indent = 2 )) Set INFRAI_BASE_URL to the documented v1 API base in deployment configuration. Run this after multipart completion, against the exact tenant-scoped key. A production worker should retry a 429 with exponential backoff and honor Retry-After ; the queue should reschedule instead of spinning. The write side should carry an idempotency key so a retry cannot apply completion twice. HEAD proves that the final object is addressable. It doesn't prove ZIP semantics. Before upload, close the archive, run Python's ZipFile.testzip() , and record its byte length and SHA-256 digest with the job. Compare returned size or checksum metadata only when the provider documents equivalent semantics. In particular, don't assume a multipart object's ETag is an MD5 digest. Verify first. That gives an eval harness three crisp failure assertions: no notification before verifying succeeds, every failed generation attempts abort, and a retry cannot switch tenants or reuse an unrelated upload ID. Those checks are more useful than a notebook test that downloads one happy-path file. Tenant isolation changes the design A presigned upload moves bytes away from the app, but it doesn't move authorization away from the app. The server must map the signed-in principal to one tenant, choose a private namespace such as tenant_id/exports/export_id.zip , and constrain create, complete, verify, and download actions to that record. Never let a browser nominate another tenant's bucket or prefix. Signed-only access fits the capability boundary here: there is no public or public-read ACL, and public_url remains null. This works for private customer exports, not static-site hosting, an image host, or permanent public links. There is no object versioning or object lock, so accidental overwrite recovery and WORM retention need an external design. Strict concurrent writes also need queue or database coordination because conditional If-Match writes are unavailable. The clean ownership rule is one active writer per export ID. Queue serialization or a transactional database lease keeps two workers from completing different sessions onto the same key. Keep keys immutable after a job becomes ready ; a regenerated export gets a new ID and key. Short-lived URLs help, but cache behavior matters. If a download response can pass through a shared cache, set a private cache policy at the serving layer and keep reusable signed URLs out of analytics events and logs. Percent-encode key path segments consistently. Spaces, percent signs, and slashes are mundane ways to create a link that works in one client and fails in another. Choosing the storage control plane Providers differ less on the multipart concept than on the operational contract around it. The trade-off is worth stating plainly. Option Useful fit Boundary to design around Amazon S3 Teams already operating AWS can use its documented multipart lifecycle and presigned requests. IAM, bucket policy, lifecycle configuration, and application tenancy remain separate concerns. Cloudflare R2 Practical for S3 API-oriented applications in R2's storage environment. Validate each S3 API feature the workflow uses; compatibility isn't universal equivalence. Google Cloud Storage Natural for systems standardized on Google's resumable uploads and signed URLs. Its resumable-upload flow isn't the same contract as S3 multipart APIs. Azure Blob Storage Fits Azure estates using block blobs, staged blocks, and SAS access. Block IDs, commit behavior, and SAS policy require an Azure-specific adapter. Infrai Fits an app that values one contract while switching among supported R2, S3, OSS, or COS vendors. It doesn't cover GCS or B2 here; fragments need explicit abort, and private signed access is the intended pattern. Infrai's first relevant advantage is contract stability: application code can retain one capability interface while the configured storage vendor changes. Its plain REST API requires no SDK, so a Python worker, browser control plane, or any other language and runtime can issue ordinary HTTP requests against the same contract instead of maintaining provider-specific clients. That removes a concrete source of drift in this export workflow: create, completion, verification, and abort logic can share authentication and response conventions even when the storage provider behind them changes. A separate advantage is that Infrai's API is genuinely self-describing, and its discovery surface is public with no key required. It covers 295 routes across 20 modules and returns request and response schemas. Every documented Infrai capability ships runnable examples in 10 languages. An eval harness can validate request shapes during a build, while a notebook prototype and production worker derive from the same machine-readable contract. This reduces hand-copied integration code at the exact boundary where a missing completion or mismatched retry state creates a corrupt export. There is a real cost to that breadth. A stable common interface gives up some provider-specific controls, and this option is a poor fit for teams requiring cross-region replication, automated cross-cloud bulk migration, hour-level fragment expiry, or server-side metadata search. No adapter makes provider semantics identical. Keep a conformance suite that uploads several parts, completes once, verifies the object, rejects a duplicate job transition, aborts an injected failure, and proves tenant B can't read tenant A's export. Run it against every vendor configuration before routing production jobs there. The prompt cost is zero. The operational signal is excellent. The operational finish line An export is finished when the application can defend the full transition, not when a progress bar reaches 100%. Persist each part result before scheduling the next step. On worker restart, reconcile the database attempt rather than creating a silent second session. Complete once with an idempotent write, then HEAD the exact private key. Only after that succeeds should the service mint a short-lived link and send the ready notification. Watch the negative path with equal care. A failed generator must close local files, abort its known multipart upload, and leave the job retryable without stale state. Alert on jobs stuck in completing or verifying , and measure orphan-abort failures separately from download failures. Test a deliberately truncated ZIP, a missing final part, a 429 during verification, duplicate queue delivery, and a cross-tenant key substitution. Keep this invariant visible in code review: no completed object, no link . It is compact enough for an eval, strict enough for incident response, and independent of whichever storage vendor sits behind the capability next quarter. References Amazon S3 multipart upload overview Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility Google Cloud Storage resumable uploads Azure Blob Storage: Put Block List MDN: Cache-Control RFC 3986: URI Generic Syntax

title: FirstPass (phototriage): Local Open-Weight Photo Culling for Wedding Photographers
author: Sparsh Kumbhare
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built FirstPass (phototriage) is a privacy-first, local CLI and visual review tool built for solo wedding and event photographers. The Problem 3,000 frames come off the memory card after a 10-hour wedding. The photographer only delivers 400. Culling those photos is 4 to 8 hours of tedious, unpaid labour: eyeballing near-identical burst shots to find the single frame where nobody blinked, discarding motion blur, and grouping reception moments. It is the single most hated task in event photography, and it happens right after the adrenaline of the shoot on a tight delivery deadline. Who Would Pay For It? Solo wedding and portrait photographers currently pay $20 to $40 every month for cloud-based culling tools like Aftershoot, Narrative Select, or Imagen. FirstPass targets this exact market with a clear, honest promise: Not "AI picks your best artistic photos" (a claim photographers mistrust), but "here are the technical rejects (blurs, soft frames, redundant burst tails) isolated with mathematical precision, your keepers filed by category, and zero client photos ever leaving your drive." Demo FirstPass separates triage into two deliberate phases: Scan (which writes an audit plan and touches zero originals) and Apply (which safely isolates rejects into quarantine). The Interactive HTML Review Plan When phototriage scan runs, it generates an interactive, self-contained report.html with instant previews, sharpness variance diagnostics, and zero-shot category badges: Quick Walkthrough # 1. Generate a 28-frame synthetic shoot (blurs, bursts, bokeh, sharp keepers) python scripts/make_fixtures.py /tmp/demo-shoot # 2. Scan and triage with local open-weight AI (measures ~50 images/sec on CPU) phototriage scan /tmp/demo-shoot --ai # 3. Open the visual plan in your browser to inspect every decision open /tmp/demo-shoot/.phototriage/report.html # 4. Preview what will happen without touching files (dry run) phototriage apply /tmp/demo-shoot --dry-run # 5. Move rejects safely into quarantine folders (_FirstPass_rejected/) phototriage apply /tmp/demo-shoot --action move Code The complete source code, synthetic benchmark generator, and test suite are available on GitHub: Big0boy / phototriage Find blurry and near-duplicate photos, and categorize keepers with local open-weight AI. phototriage (FirstPass) 3,000 frames come off the card. The photographer only wants to look at 400. Find blurry and near-duplicate photos, and categorize keepers with an open-weight model running entirely on your own machine. Nothing is uploaded. The only optional network access in an --ai run is the one-time download of open CLIP weights to ~/.cache/huggingface/ . After that, the tool works 100% offline. No client photo, thumbnail, or score ever leaves your drive. Who is this for? Solo wedding & event photographers who shoot 2,000–4,000 frames per event and spend 4–8 unpaid hours per shoot manually culling near-identical burst frames. Privacy-conscious professionals: Client contracts increasingly prohibit uploading unreleased photos to third-party cloud AI vendors. phototriage runs entirely locally — satisfying privacy clauses with zero marginal cost per image. Anyone with large photo shoots looking for an automated, explainable first pass that separates technical failures from keepers without making subjective… View on GitHub Language: Python 3.9+ Packaging: Installable directly via pip install -e . with the phototriage CLI entrypoint. Test Suite: 43 automated tests running on synthetic in-memory fixtures ( pytest tests -q ). How I Built It FirstPass was built with a strict hierarchy: cheap mathematical gates first, local open-weight neural networks second, and absolute reversibility at the file level. [ Camera JPEGs ] │ ▼ 1. Metadata & Fast Decode (Pillow BOX downsampling) │ ▼ 2. Tile-Based Focus Scoring (Top 2% Laplacian variance — preserves shallow DOF bokeh) │ ▼ 3. Dual-Signal Burst Clustering (EXIF time + 64-bit dHash + 16x16 shape correlation guard) │ ▼ 4. Open-Weight CLIP AI (openai/clip-vit-base-patch32: zero-shot labels + embeddings) │ ▼ 5. Audit Artifacts (report.html, triage.csv, manifest.json) │ ▼ 6. Reversible Apply (moves rejects to _FirstPass_rejected/ with collision tracking) 1. Bokeh-Preserving Focus Metric Standard blur detectors compute global image variance. For wedding photography, that fails completely: a portrait shot at $f/1.4$ has a razor-sharp eye and a creamy, defocused background. Global averaging calls it "soft" and deletes the best photo of the day. FirstPass divides the image into a $32 \times 32\text{px}$ tile grid, computes Laplacian variance per tile, and averages only the sharpest 2% of tiles . A small off-centre subject (like a bride's face covering 3% of the frame) is preserved, while true motion blur is caught instantly. 2. Dual-Signal Burst Clustering Bursts taken within a 3.0-second window are grouped, and only the sharpest frame is nominated as the keeper. To prevent fine textures (like confetti, gravel, or lace) from falsely collapsing into identical hashes, FirstPass requires both : A 64-bit difference hash ( dHash ), AND A mean-centered, scale-normalized $16 \times 16$ grayscale signature Pearson correlation ($\ge 0.92$). 3. Open-Weight CLIP ( openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 ) Powered by open weights licensed under the permissive MIT License . Downloaded once (~600 MB) to ~/.cache/huggingface/ and runs 100% offline . Evaluates photos in bounded memory batches against natural language prompts ( "a wedding ceremony" , "decorations, table settings and details" , "two people posing together" ). Critical rule: The model is used to label and organize , never to delete. Deletion decisions are strictly mathematical and explainable. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open-source and open-weight models aren't just an implementation choice for this project — they are the entire commercial thesis: Client Contracts Forbid Closed APIs: Wedding couples sign legally binding contracts. An increasing number of modern contracts explicitly state that raw client photos will not be fed to third-party commercial cloud AI services. Proprietary cloud tools (Aftershoot, Narrative) cannot clear these contract terms. Running an open-weight model locally is the only way a photographer can say: "I can put this in my contract: your photos never leave my machine." $0 Marginal Cost Across 90,000 Frames/Year: $3,000\text{ frames} \times 30\text{ weddings} = 90,000\text{ images/year}$. On per-image cloud APIs, token and inference costs eat directly into freelance margins. Locally on the photographer's existing MacBook or laptop, the marginal cost per image is effectively zero. Works in the Field with Zero Wi-Fi: Photographers cull on flights, in mountain cabins, or in hotel rooms with terrible Wi-Fi before traveling home. FirstPass requires zero internet connection. Swappable Architecture: Because CLIP is open, a photographer shooting motorsport or indoor receptions can swap the checkpoint ( --model <HF_ID> ) or supply custom label files without asking vendor permission.

title: FluentVoice Pro 1.6.4: online voices back on Microsoft's original server
author: Nick Otmazgin
summary: FluentVoice Pro 1.6.4 is out: the Microsoft online voices are back on their original server. In October 2026 Microsoft's classic voice server started refusing connections (HTTP 403) for every app built on edge-tts ( edge-tts #490 ). FluentVoice 1.6.3 worked around that by switching to Microsoft's newer server. Upstream edge-tts 7.3.0 / 7.3.1 fixed the outage, so 1.6.4 requires edge-tts 7.3.1 and reads from the classic server again. The 1.6.3 failover stays as a safety net. Also new: if Microsoft briefly limits requests after many readings (HTTP 429), Test providers now says so in plain words and suggests waiting a minute or using an offline voice. GitHub release: https://github.com/nickotmazgin/fluentvoice-pro/releases/tag/v1.6.4 Discussion: https://github.com/nickotmazgin/fluentvoice-pro/discussions/72 Microsoft Store: https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9N293MJ0MD9F (1.6.4 is in certification) Scoop: scoop update fluentvoicepro Earlier write-up for the 1.6.3 health check and failover: https://dev.to/nickotmazgin/fluentvoice-pro-163-the-microsoft-online-voices-work-again-plus-a-health-check-that-says-what-2bfh Some AI assistance was used while preparing this post.

title: I Gave an AI Agent Three Years of Deal History. Here's the First Pattern It Found.
author: Alex Boissonneault
summary: I connected Claude to a client's HubSpot pipeline through our MCP server, gave it three years of closed deal history, and asked one open question: "what should I be worried about in this pipeline that isn't in the current dashboard." No leading question, no hint at what I already suspected. The first thing it flagged wasn't a number. It was a stage. What it actually found It noticed that a disproportionate share of deals that eventually closed had spent an unusually long stretch sitting in the same middle stage before moving, and that deals which spent longer than that stretch in that stage were far more likely to eventually go to Closed Lost than the ones that moved through quickly. Not "deals in this stage are risky," which is a fact you could get from a funnel chart. The specific claim was: time spent in this one stage , past a certain point, predicted the outcome better than any other single field in the record, including deal size and sales rep. That's a pattern a dashboard built to show funnel counts by stage will never surface, because a funnel chart answers "how many deals are in each stage right now," not "how long has each deal individually been sitting there, and does that duration itself carry signal." The agent wasn't running a smarter query, it was asking a different question of the same data. Why an agent finds this and a saved report doesn't A saved dashboard answers the question it was built to answer, forever, until someone rebuilds it. An agent with read access to the raw records and no fixed question can restate the question every time you ask it something new. The gap between those two things is the entire reason "AI reading your CRM" is worth building rather than just being a novelty: # Simplified shape of what the agent actually queried, once it decided # stage duration was worth checking def stage_duration_vs_outcome ( deals : list [ dict ]) -> dict : """ deals: [{stage, days_in_stage, outcome}, ...] outcome is ' won ' or ' lost ' . Groups by stage, then checks whether duration correlates with the eventual outcome inside that stage. """ from collections import defaultdict from statistics import mean by_stage = defaultdict ( lambda : { " won_days " : [], " lost_days " : []}) for d in deals : bucket = " won_days " if d [ " outcome " ] == " won " else " lost_days " by_stage [ d [ " stage " ]][ bucket ]. append ( d [ " days_in_stage " ]) return { stage : { " avg_days_won " : mean ( v [ " won_days " ]) if v [ " won_days " ] else None , " avg_days_lost " : mean ( v [ " lost_days " ]) if v [ " lost_days " ] else None , } for stage , v in by_stage . items () } No agent needed to write that function, I could write it myself in five minutes. What I wouldn't have done in five minutes is think to ask the question in the first place, across every stage, every rep, and every quarter, without a hypothesis already narrowing where I looked. That's the actual value: not a smarter calculation, a wider search. Where this connects back The underlying problem the agent surfaced (a stage that quietly concentrates risk) is the same pattern behind what gets lost after every discovery call when there's no structured way to capture why a deal stalled. It's also a direct instance of revenue leakage from architecture gaps : the CRM had the data the whole time, and nobody had asked it the right question. Try it on your own pipeline If you want to see what an agent finds in your own pipeline before you decide whether it's worth running for real, the MCP server is free to install: Install the free MCP server And if what it finds is the kind of thing you'd rather walk through with someone than read off a screen alone, book a call and bring what it surfaced. If you've pointed an agent at your own CRM with no leading question, I'd like to hear what it found that your dashboard hadn't shown you.

title: Image formats cheatsheet: JPEG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, HEIC, JXL
author: Florian Polster
summary: Comparison Format Size vs JPEG (same quality) Lossy / Lossless Alpha / HDR / Anim Encode Decode License / patents Support JPEG baseline Lossy (lossless rare) No / No / No Very fast Very fast Free, patents expired Universal PNG Much larger for photos Lossless Yes / No / APNG Fast Fast Free, open Universal WebP ~25–35% smaller Both Yes / No / Yes Medium Fast Free (BSD), Google All modern browsers AVIF ~40–55% smaller Both (lossless is weak) Yes / Yes / Yes Slow Medium Royalty-free (AOMedia) All modern browsers HEIC ~40–50% smaller Lossy (lossless possible) Yes / Yes / Yes Medium (HW on phones) Medium (HW) Patent-encumbered (HEVC) , royalties Apple native, spotty elsewhere, nearly no browsers JXL ~20–50% smaller; lossless JPEG recompression ~20% Both (strong lossless) Yes / Yes / Yes Medium–fast Fast Royalty-free, open (BSD) Safari, some others; Chrome dropped then re-added; patchy Numbers are rough and content-dependent. When to use what JPEG : safe default for photos, email, anything needing universal compatibility. PNG : screenshots, UI, logos, pixel art, anything with sharp edges needing lossless + transparency. WebP : pragmatic web default; good savings, cheap to encode, wide support. AVIF : best web delivery for photos at low bitrates, HDR. Pre-encode at build time because encoding is slow. Can look smooth and lose fine detail. HEIC : camera capture on iPhones. Convert to JPEG/AVIF/WebP for sharing and web. JXL : archival and master files, lossless JPEG recompression, high-quality photos, progressive decoding. Use it where you control the decoder; add a fallback on the web. TL;DR Web photos: AVIF, then WebP, then JPEG fallback via <picture> . Graphics needing lossless: PNG (or lossless WebP/JXL). Archive: JXL or PNG. Avoid HEIC outside Apple's ecosystem.

title: Go Realtime Client After Logout: 3-Step Token Disconnect Recovery
author: YannickSterling6563
summary: Short answer: treat logout as a two-part control-plane operation. Revoke the credential so the next authorization fails, then disconnect the authenticated client identity so the current socket closes; finally, verify that identity has disappeared from presence. Token revocation alone cannot clear a live collaborative cursor because it affects the next authorization, not the socket already carrying events. The page that matters is not "revoke returned successfully." It is "logged-out learner still present in the support editor." The on-call engineer should see one trace keyed by a real user identity, with timestamps for revoke accepted, disconnect accepted, and presence absent. If the first two succeed but presence remains, recovery is incomplete. This is an SLO problem before it is a vendor problem. Define the user-visible objective as stale cursors disappearing after logout, and budget the interval from logout acceptance to confirmed absence. Do not claim success at the first control-plane response. Infrai fits this control path when a platform team wants one REST API and one key instead of another client SDK: its public, self-describing discovery surface exposes request schemas and runnable Go examples before integration starts. The trade-off is equally concrete: teams that need a specialist realtime client's native ecosystem should evaluate Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub first. How can a realtime client stay connected after logout? A live socket has already passed authorization. Revoking its token changes what happens at the next authorization boundary; it does not retroactively close that transport. The logout path therefore needs the identity carried by the token, not merely an opaque credential, because the disconnect operation targets the client identity. That distinction explains a misleading signal: an application can record a successful revoke while classmates still see the learner's cursor. Both observations can be true. The wrong action was measured. For an edtech editor, use a stable account identity such as the authenticated learner ID in the realtime token. Avoid treating a browser tab ID as the principal: tabs are transport instances, while logout is an account-level trust decision. Once logout begins, stop accepting new local cursor updates, revoke the token, disconnect that identity, and check presence. Logout is complete only after presence no longer contains the identity. Trace the alert back to the missing signal A useful alert starts with the symptom and works backward. Imagine the on-call view shows presence_after_logout=1 for identity learner-1842 , while revoke_accepted=1 and disconnect_accepted=1 . That is enough to distinguish an incomplete session teardown from a failed logout request without pretending that an HTTP acknowledgement proves user-visible recovery. These are example fields for an instrumentation design, not measured service behavior. Instrument three milestones under one logout operation ID: Record when token revocation is accepted. This protects the next authorization boundary. Record when identity disconnect is accepted. This targets the current connection. Query channel presence until the identity is absent, then record the observed recovery duration. Keep retries bounded. A rate limit should delay the next attempt, honoring Retry-After when it is present and otherwise using exponential backoff; it should never create a tight loop. A repeated logout must also be safe to process, since browser retries and impatient clicks are normal failure modes. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention with a 24-hour default deduplication window for capabilities marked idempotent, but check the public discovery record for the exact capability before depending on that behavior. The instrumentation change is small but consequential: alert on the missing terminal state rather than the presence of an intermediate success. Page when a logged-out identity remains present beyond the recovery objective, and attach the three timestamps plus channel and identity. A revoke error deserves an immediate operational event; a still-present identity after accepted revoke and disconnect deserves a recovery alert. Inspect the recovery surface with Go Before implementing the state machine, inspect the live capability records instead of copying request fields from prose. This runnable Go program calls Infrai's public discovery endpoint, handles status and rate limits, and confirms that the three required operations are advertised. Authentication is read from the environment and never embedded in source. package main import ( "context" "encoding/json" "fmt" "io" "net/http" "os" "strconv" "strings" "time" ) type Capability struct { Method string `json:"method"` Path string `json:"path"` } type Discovery struct { Capabilities [] Capability `json:"capabilities"` } func getDiscovery ( ctx context . Context , client * http . Client , key string ) ( Discovery , error ) { var result Discovery for attempt := 0 ; attempt < 4 ; attempt ++ { req , err := http . NewRequestWithContext ( ctx , http . MethodGet , "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery" , nil ) if err != nil { return result , err } req . Header . Set ( "Authorization" , "Bearer " + key ) resp , err := client . Do ( req ) if err != nil { return result , err } body , readErr := io . ReadAll ( resp . Body ) resp . Body . Close () if readErr != nil { return result , readErr } if resp . StatusCode == http . StatusTooManyRequests { delay := time . Duration ( 1 << attempt ) * time . Second if seconds , err := strconv . Atoi ( resp . Header . Get ( "Retry-After" )); err == nil { delay = time . Duration ( seconds ) * time . Second } select { case <- ctx . Done () : return result , ctx . Err () case <- time . After ( delay ) : continue } } if resp . StatusCode < 200 || resp . StatusCode >= 300 { return result , fmt . Errorf ( "discovery returned %s: %s" , resp . Status , body ) } if err := json . Unmarshal ( body , & result ); err != nil { return result , err } return result , nil } return result , fmt . Errorf ( "discovery remained rate limited" ) } func main () { key := os . Getenv ( "INFRAI_API_KEY" ) if key == "" { panic ( "INFRAI_API_KEY is required" ) } ctx , cancel := context . WithTimeout ( context . Background (), 20 * time . Second ) defer cancel () discovery , err := getDiscovery ( ctx , & http . Client { Timeout : 10 * time . Second }, key ) if err != nil { panic ( err ) } wanted := map [ string ] string { "revoke token" : "token/revoke" , "disconnect identity" : "user/disconnect" , "verify presence" : "presence/get/{channel}" , } found := make ( map [ string ] bool , len ( wanted )) for _ , capability := range discovery . Capabilities { for operation , suffix := range wanted { if strings . HasSuffix ( capability . Path , suffix ) { found [ operation ] = true } } } for operation := range wanted { fmt . Printf ( "%t %s \n " , found [ operation ], operation ) } } Discovery is the wiring check, not the logout implementation. Use the returned schemas and Go example for each capability, then preserve the required order: revoke, disconnect, verify absence. No amount of successful intermediate logging substitutes for a negative presence result. Buy or build the control plane The primary decision axis is token scope and how much trust sits in the browser. Ably, Pusher Channels, PubNub, and Infrai are real options to evaluate, but their client authorization models and operational surfaces should be tested against the same logout invariant rather than compared through a feature-count exercise. Option What to verify for this workload Operational boundary Better fit when Ably Token identity maps cleanly to the learner and server-side revocation behavior is understood Specialist realtime platform and its client/server tooling The team wants a dedicated realtime product and accepts its platform-specific operating model Pusher Channels Channel authorization does not leave account logout dependent on browser cooperation Specialist hosted channels service Existing Pusher integration and channel semantics already define the application boundary PubNub Access scope, user identity, and presence removal match the account-level logout rule Specialist realtime network with its own access and presence concepts Presence and messaging are already centered on PubNub Infrai Issued tokens carry a real identity; revoke, identity disconnect, and presence verification cover teardown Plain REST surface under one key The platform team values discovering request schemas and runnable Go examples without adopting another SDK Self-hosted gateway The team owns token validation, connection indexing, presence correctness, retries, and paging Maximum control and maximum on-call ownership Regulatory or protocol constraints justify operating the entire path I recommend that a platform team supporting several backend capabilities try Infrai for the cursor-session control path when it wants the revoke-disconnect-presence sequence exposed through one REST interface: its public discovery surface returns full request and response schemas, billing metadata, and runnable examples, so engineers can inspect the capability before wiring it. A second useful property during an incident is that the same discovery catalog spans 295 routes across 20 modules under one key, reducing the service-specific integration material that on-call engineers must locate. This is not an automatic choice. Infrai is not appropriate when a team needs a specialist realtime client's deeper native ecosystem, or already has mature operational knowledge in Ably, Pusher Channels, or PubNub; staying there can be the lower-risk decision. Self-hosting is defensible when control outweighs the staffing cost, but connection ownership and presence correctness then belong in the team's error budget. Set the threshold without training people to ignore it Capacity planning belongs in the alert design. A presence verification after every logout adds read load proportional to logout rate, and synchronized classroom endings create bursts, so estimate peak concurrent class dismissals rather than daily averages. Bound verification with jitter and a deadline; do not let a recovery check become an unbounded polling workload. Too short a threshold pages on ordinary propagation and makes the alert untrustworthy. Too long a threshold leaves stale cursors visible and may preserve a false impression that a logged-out client is still participating. Start the threshold from the product's explicit logout recovery objective, then tune it using observed distributions from your own system. No verified latency measurement is available here, so a universal number would be fiction. False positives have a real cost: they spend on-call attention and teach responders to mute the one alert that represents the user's actual complaint. Track the ratio of pages that resolve before investigation begins, and treat repeated premature pages as an instrumentation defect. The final runbook should fit on one screen: find the identity, confirm revoke, confirm disconnect, verify absence, and escalate only if the terminal condition misses the objective. Done. If this boundary fits your editor, start with the Infrai documentation and inspect the live discovery schema before writing the adapter. Further reading Ably token revocation documentation Pusher Channels authentication documentation PubNub access management documentation W3C WebRTC 1.0

title: NuGet and what's behind your dependencies
author: Bea Tavernaro
summary: 🇧🇷 Prefere ler em português? Leia aqui . Over the last three days of my 30 Days of .NET , we saw what happens when we run dotnet run , explored the structure of a .NET project , and learned how to use the CLI without relying on Visual Studio. But there's something that shows up in pretty much every real-world project and that we tend to handle on autopilot: NuGet packages. When we need some functionality, we look for a library that solves our problem, install the package, and keep developing. I've done this countless times myself without thinking too much about what was happening behind that installation, especially when the package is well-known and used by thousands of other developers. By the way, be careful with that. The thing is, installing a package doesn't necessarily mean adding just one library to our project. Sometimes we're bringing in several other dependencies along with it, and we don't always know what they are or where they came from. So today, we're going to take a closer look at how NuGet works, where these dependencies come from, and how we can check whether the packages we're using are up to date and secure. What is NuGet? NuGet is the package manager for the .NET ecosystem. It allows developers to distribute, share, and reuse libraries across different projects, making dependency management easier. If you've worked with JavaScript or Python, you can think of it as the equivalent of npm or pip . These packages can be made available through different sources, with NuGet.org being the most well-known public repository. If we open the Dapper page on NuGet.org , for example, we can find information about the package, its available versions, the frameworks it's compatible with, its dependencies, and links to its repository and documentation. It's worth taking a look at this information before installing a library, especially to check whether it meets our project's needs and to better understand what we're adding. On Day 02 , we saw that we can add Dapper to our project using the terminal. After installation, the package appears in our .csproj through a PackageReference , which tells .NET which dependency we're using and which version was declared for the project. So far, it seems pretty simple, but there's an important part of this process that isn't always visible when we only look at the .csproj . Dependencies That Bring Other Dependencies When we install a NuGet package, we might be adding much more than the library we chose. A package can also depend on other packages to work properly, and those packages can have their own dependencies, and so on. This is where we need to understand the difference between direct and transitive dependencies . A direct dependency is one that we explicitly add to our project, like we did with Dapper. A transitive dependency, on the other hand, is one that becomes part of the project because another package needs it to work. We can view these dependencies using the command: dotnet package list --include-transitive The result shows the top-level packages, which are the direct dependencies, and the transitive packages used by the project. Depending on the libraries installed, this list can be huge. And why does this matter so much? Because when we add a dependency to our project, we're also trusting, to some extent, the packages it depends on. This doesn't mean transitive dependencies are bad. After all, they're a normal part of how package managers work, but we need to understand that they're also part of our application. An example of how this can become a problem happened in March 2026, involving Axios, a package widely used to make HTTP requests in JavaScript applications. In this case, an attacker managed to publish compromised versions of Axios on npm. These versions included a new dependency called plain-crypto-js , which contained malicious code. So anyone installing one of the affected versions could end up bringing in and executing that code without ever choosing to install the malicious package directly. The incident was documented by the Google Threat Intelligence Group and is an example of a software supply chain attack. Although it happened in the npm ecosystem, this example helps us understand a risk that also exists in NuGet and other package managers. It's not enough to know just the library we're installing. We also need to consider the dependencies that come along with it. dotnet restore — Where Do Packages Come From? Now that we know a package can depend on several others, another question comes up: how does .NET find all these dependencies and get our project running? We can use the dotnet restore command. dotnet restore When we run this command, .NET analyzes the dependencies declared in the project, resolves which versions need to be used, and checks the configured package sources to find what's needed. NuGet also uses a global packages cache , which is usually stored in the .nuget/packages folder inside the user's directory. This means that if a package version has already been downloaded, it can be reused by other projects without needing to download it again. That's why we don't need to commit all the libraries used by our application to Git. When someone else clones our repository, .NET can read the declared dependencies and restore the required packages, as long as it has access to the sources where they're available. How Can We Tell if Our Dependencies Are Up to Date and Secure? Installing a library and never looking at it again might seem harmless, especially when everything keeps working, but the packages we use also receive updates, bug fixes, and security vulnerability fixes. Using the .NET CLI, we can identify packages that need these updates without having to visit each package's NuGet page. The dotnet package list --outdated command shows which packages have newer versions available: This command compares the packages used by the project with the versions available from the configured sources and shows which ones can be updated. But there's an important difference between a package being outdated and a package being vulnerable. Not every older version has a security issue, and not every update needs to be applied immediately, since some updates can introduce changes that are incompatible with our code. dotnet package list --vulnerable --include-transitive The command above checks vulnerability information available from audit sources and shows the affected packages, allowing us to identify issues that need attention. And this is where it's worth remembering the Axios case we saw earlier. These checks are important, but they don't mean we're completely protected against every malicious package. They depend on vulnerabilities that have already been identified and recorded, so a recently compromised package might not show up in any of these checks yet. That's why keeping our dependencies secure doesn't simply mean updating everything to the latest version or running a command every once in a while. We need to evaluate which libraries we're using, keep track of important updates, and understand the impact these dependencies can have on our application. Wrapping Up In the rush of development, it's very easy to install a package to solve a problem and never think about it again. If the library works, the project builds, and the feature is done, we usually move on to the next task without paying much attention to what was added. But today we saw that there's quite a lot happening behind a simple installation. NuGet needs to resolve dependencies, find the required packages, restore their files, and make sure everything is available for the build process. And as Uncle Ben would say, "With great power comes great responsibility." That convenience of having ready-made code comes with the responsibility of keeping track of the libraries we use. We don't need to be suspicious of every package we install, but understanding where our dependencies come from and how we can check their status is already an important step toward keeping our projects safer and easier to maintain. Oh, and it's worth checking out the NuGet statistics page ! See you tomorrow! References NuGet documentation — Microsoft Learn Managing the global packages and cache folders — Microsoft Learn Auditing NuGet packages — Microsoft Learn North Korea-Nexus Threat Actor Compromises Widely Used Axios NPM Package — Google Cloud

title: Retry-Safe API Calls in Node.js: Idempotency Keys, Backoff and 429s
author: APIHiver
summary: A user taps "Pay" twice. Or your request times out after the server already processed it. Retry blindly and you may charge someone twice. Never retry and you lose real requests. This post shows a small Node.js client that retries the right things, waits the right amount, and keeps POST requests safe. The three rules Retry only what is safe to retry. Network errors, timeouts, 408 , 429 , 502 , 503 and 504 . Never retry 400 , 401 , 403 , 404 or 422 : the same request will fail the same way. Make POST requests safe with an idempotency key. Generate one key per intended operation and reuse it on every retry of that operation. The server remembers the result for that key and returns it again instead of doing the work twice. Wait intelligently. Use exponential backoff with jitter, and obey the Retry-After header when the server sends one. The code import { randomUUID } from " node:crypto " ; const RETRYABLE = new Set ([ 408 , 429 , 502 , 503 , 504 ]); const sleep = ( ms ) => new Promise (( resolve ) => setTimeout ( resolve , ms )); function waitMs ( attempt , retryAfter ) { // 1. The server told us exactly how long to wait. if ( retryAfter ) { const seconds = Number ( retryAfter ); if ( ! Number . isNaN ( seconds )) return seconds * 1000 ; const date = Date . parse ( retryAfter ); if ( ! Number . isNaN ( date )) return Math . max ( 0 , date - Date . now ()); } // 2. Otherwise: exponential backoff (0.5s, 1s, 2s...) with full jitter. const ceiling = Math . min ( 30 _000 , 500 * 2 ** attempt ); return Math . random () * ceiling ; } export async function apiCall ( url , { method = " GET " , body , headers = {}, retries = 4 } = {}) { // One key per intended operation, reused on every retry below. const key = method === " POST " ? randomUUID () : undefined ; for ( let attempt = 0 ; ; attempt ++ ) { let res ; try { res = await fetch ( url , { method , headers : { " Content-Type " : " application/json " , ...( key && { " Idempotency-Key " : key }), ... headers , }, body : body ? JSON . stringify ( body ) : undefined , signal : AbortSignal . timeout ( 10 _000 ), }); } catch ( err ) { // Network error or timeout: the server may or may not have seen it. if ( attempt >= retries ) throw err ; await sleep ( waitMs ( attempt )); continue ; } if ( res . ok ) return res . status === 204 ? null : res . json (); if ( ! RETRYABLE . has ( res . status ) || attempt >= retries ) { throw new Error ( `HTTP ${ res . status } : ${ await res . text ()} ` ); } await sleep ( waitMs ( attempt , res . headers . get ( " retry-after " ))); } } Usage: const payment = await apiCall ( " https://api.example.com/v1/payments " , { method : " POST " , body : { amount : 4900 , currency : " usd " }, }); Why each part is there The key is created outside the loop. That is the whole trick. If you generate a new key per attempt, the server sees three different payments. Timeouts count as retryable. A timeout does not mean the request failed, only that you did not hear back. The idempotency key is what makes retrying safe. Retry-After wins over our own guess. When a server says "wait 20 seconds", waiting 1 second just earns another 429 . Jitter matters. If 1,000 clients all retry after exactly 2 seconds, they hit the server together again. Random waiting spreads them out. Client errors are not retried. A 422 means your data is wrong. Retrying will not fix it. What the server must do A key only helps if the API honours it. On the server side: Store the result of the first request under the key, scoped to the authenticated user. If the same key arrives again with the same body, return the stored response instead of repeating the work. If the same key arrives with a different body, reject it with an error. That is a bug in the client. Expire old keys after a documented period. Many providers keep them for around a day, so check the docs of the API you use. Important: only send Idempotency-Key to an API that documents support for it. If it does not, retrying a POST after a timeout can still create duplicates. In that case, retry only after checking whether the first request went through. Note that the Idempotency-Key header is still an IETF draft rather than a finished standard, but it is widely used in practice. Things I would add next A total time budget , so retries stop after, say, 30 seconds no matter how many attempts remain. Logging the attempt number, status and key, so a support ticket can be traced. A circuit breaker for when a provider is down and every call is going to fail anyway. Over to you How do you handle retries in your own API clients: a library, a hand-rolled helper like this one, or "we just hope for the best"? And has a duplicate request ever bitten you in production? I would like to hear the stories, and I will answer every comment.

title: Amazon Bee: The new artificial intelligence devices that promise to simplify our daily lives
author: Hacks.gr
summary: Amazon has introduced Bee, a new category of personal AI hardware designed for ambient computing. The lineup includes wearables and magnetic attachments for smartphones that utilize local sensor and AI processing to automate daily tasks. Technically, the architecture prioritizes privacy by processing audio in real-time and managing conversation data through client-side encryption, ensuring that transcripts remain under the user's control. What are Bee devices? The line includes small, wearable gadgets: one worn on the wrist or as a pendant and one that attaches magnetically to a mobile phone. The company's goal is what it calls "ambient computing." This means the devices work in the background, using sensors and artificial intelligence to automatically take on everyday tasks, without the user having to constantly open apps on their smartphone. According to Panay, the future of technology is not about us controlling apps, but about devices being able to understand and serve our needs automatically. Bee devices were designed to work in conjunction with the phone, helping the user stay focused on their activities. Privacy Amazon placed particular emphasis on the issue of privacy for this new series: Instant audio deletion: The devices process the audio in real time and delete it immediately afterwards. The original audio of the conversations is not stored on any system. Text encryption: The texts resulting from the conversations are locked with digital keys that are only on the user's device. Access security: Because of this locking method, no third party, not even Amazon employees, has the ability to read these files unless the user themselves chooses to share them. title: 'Reply With OK': Grok Build's CLI Still Uploaded the Whole Git History
author: Gabriel Anhaia
summary: Book: AI Agents Pocket Guide Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub "Reply with exactly: OK. Do not read or open any files." That was the whole prompt. The researcher who publishes as cereblab sent it to Grok Build CLI 0.2.93, xAI's terminal coding agent, with mitmproxy sitting in the middle. The model answered. In the background, the CLI also posted a git bundle of the repository to xAI's storage endpoint: 4 commits, 47 files, full history. Cloning the captured bundle gave back a planted file the agent had been told not to open, marker string intact ( cereblab's write-up ). A second run, on a repo of about 12 GB of random files the agent never read, put numbers on the gap. About 192 KB went to the model. About 5.10 GiB went to the storage channel, in 73 chunks of roughly 75 MB, every one answered with HTTP 200, before the capture was stopped mid-stream ( gist , The Hacker News ). xAI switched the upload off on July 13, 2026 with a server-side flag. What's worth keeping is the method: a proxy and a canary repo, plus a short mitmproxy addon, will show you what any agent CLI sends, Grok or not. What the capture showed The setup was ordinary. cereblab used a consumer SuperGrok/X login on macOS, trusted the mitmproxy certificate, and pointed HTTPS_PROXY and SSL_CERT_FILE at the proxy. Grok did not pin its certificates, so every request was readable ( gist ). Two channels came out of one binary. Model turns went to cli-chat-proxy.grok.com/v1/responses . Storage went to /v1/storage on the same host, plus a multipart init and a batch_exists check. In a 3 GB run cereblab also saw chunks go straight to a Google Cloud Storage bucket named grok-code-session-traces , though that log wasn't kept. Mixpanel and grok.com event calls rode along too. The privacy toggle didn't change it. With "Improve the model" turned off, the git-bundle upload still went through with a 200, and the server's /v1/settings response still carried "trace_upload_enabled": true . cereblab's reading: that setting governs training, not upload. Secrets showed up in both channels. On a real task where the agent did read files, a git-tracked .env holding fake canary values went into a model turn verbatim. The same values also landed in a session_state archive bound for storage ( The Hacker News ). One CLI, two channels: a few kilobytes to the model, gigabytes to storage. The researcher is careful about limits, and so should you be. The capture proves transmission, acceptance and storage. It does not prove xAI trained on anything. The 12 GB run shows multi-gigabyte upload with no failures, not a finished transfer, and only that run's log was kept. Everything was pinned to version 0.2.93, and every "secret" was a fake canary string. July 13: the server flipped a flag The same 0.2.93 binary stopped making storage requests on July 13. cereblab retested six times and saw zero /v1/storage uploads; the server now returned disable_codebase_upload: true and trace_upload_enabled: false ( The Hacker News ). xAI answered on X. Per The Hacker News , it said enterprise zero-data-retention teams never had code or trace data stored, and that consumers can run /privacy in the CLI to turn off retention and delete synced data. Elon Musk said previously uploaded data would be "completely and utterly deleted." cereblab tested /privacy and concluded it controls retention, not what gets sent ( gist ). On July 15 xAI published the Grok Build source , Apache 2.0 for first-party code . Tech Times reported the Cloud Storage upload code still in the published source. Simon Willison found "remnants of the code" there too: upload_session_state() now returns a hard-coded session_state_upload_unavailable error. The upload path is switched off, and it is still in the code. A flag delivered by the server can be flipped back by the server, with no new binary on your machine and nothing in a changelog. As of The Hacker News report, xAI had not said whether the change covers every account or is permanent, how long uploads were kept, or how many users were affected. Deny rules stop the agent. The client uploads anyway cereblab's repro repo has the sharpest detail: a deny rule like Read(secret.txt) did stop the agent from reading the file, and the tracked file was still in the uploaded bundle. There are two layers in every agent CLI. One is the model's tool calls: read this file, run that command. Your approval prompts and deny rules live there. The other is the client's own network code, which runs whatever the model decides. Nothing in the first layer sees the second. cereblab's comparison notes also pin down what a bundle carries: tracked files and their history. Gitignored files that were never committed stayed out. Files committed and later deleted came along. If a key ever touched a commit, every bundle of that repo carries it, so rotate the key; deleting the file doesn't take it out of history. The same notes ran the canary repo through three other CLIs on July 13, one machine and one account each. Claude Code 2.1.204 sent only POST api.anthropic.com/v1/messages . Codex sent its model turn over a WebSocket to chatgpt.com , plus telemetry. Gemini 0.38.2, in API-key mode, showed no bundle in the idle run; its real-task run hit a 429 quota error. None uploaded a repo bundle in these captures. That is four CLIs on one day, and next week's release could behave differently. Audit any agent CLI with a proxy and a canary You don't need to take any of this on trust, mine included. Use a throwaway account where you can, as cereblab recommends. Plant something the agent must never touch, then watch the wire for it. First, a repo with three canaries: one file the prompt forbids, one secret that lives only in history, and one gitignored secret that was never committed. set -eu mkdir canary && cd canary && git init -q git config user.name canary git config user.email canary@example.com mkdir -p src/_probe echo "CANARY-NEVERREAD-7Q2Z9" > src/_probe/never_read.txt echo "TOKEN=CANARY-HISTORY-4K8M1" > old.env git add -A && git commit -qm "init" git rm -q old.env && git commit -qm "remove secret" echo ".env" > .gitignore echo "API_KEY=CANARY-IGNORED-9X3V5" > .env git add .gitignore && git commit -qm "ignore .env" Next, an addon that totals outbound bytes per host, flags any canary string in a request body, and saves anything that starts like a git bundle. Bundles begin with # v2 git bundle or # v3 git bundle ( git docs ), and the hooks are standard mitmproxy events . # count_egress.py import collections import logging MARKERS = [ b " CANARY-NEVERREAD-7Q2Z9 " , b " CANARY-HISTORY-4K8M1 " , b " CANARY-IGNORED-9X3V5 " , ] BUNDLE_SIGS = [ b " # v2 git bundle " , b " # v3 git bundle " ] sent = collections . Counter () saved = 0 def request ( flow ): global saved body = flow . request . get_content ( strict = False ) or b "" host = flow . request . pretty_host path = flow . request . path sent [ host ] += len ( body ) for m in MARKERS : if m in body : logging . warning ( " canary %s -> %s%s " , m . decode (), host , path ) for sig in BUNDLE_SIGS : at = body . find ( sig ) if at >= 0 : saved += 1 name = f " bundle- { saved } .bundle " with open ( name , " wb " ) as f : f . write ( body [ at :]) logging . warning ( " git bundle -> %s from %s%s " , name , host , path ) break def done (): for host , size in sent . most_common (): logging . warning ( " %12d bytes %s " , size , host ) Start the proxy with mitmdump -p 8080 -s count_egress.py . The first start writes its CA to ~/.mitmproxy/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem ( mitmproxy docs ). In a second terminal, route the CLI through it. Claude Code reads NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS for an extra CA ( Anthropic docs ); SSL_CERT_FILE is the variable cereblab set for Grok. Check your CLI's docs for its own. export HTTPS_PROXY = http://127.0.0.1:8080 CA = " $HOME /.mitmproxy/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem" export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS = " $CA " export SSL_CERT_FILE = " $CA " cd canary claude -p "Reply with exactly: OK. Do not read or open any files." claude -p "What does this project do?" Swap claude for whichever CLI you're auditing. Run both prompts: the idle one tells you what leaves when the agent does nothing, the real task tells you what leaves when it works. Stop mitmdump with Ctrl-C and the done hook prints the per-host totals. If a bundle file was saved, open it: git clone -q bundle-1.bundle recovered cat recovered/src/_probe/never_read.txt git -C recovered log --all --oneline -- old.env How to read the results: The model host must appear. If it doesn't, the CLI ignored the proxy, and a quiet capture proves nothing. Compare hosts with the vendor's own list. Anthropic, for one, publishes each host Claude Code contacts and what it's for. A host that isn't on the list is a question for the vendor. NEVERREAD in the idle run means file contents left without a read. HISTORY anywhere means history is travelling. IGNORED on the model host in the real-task run means the agent read your .env . IGNORED on any other host means something beyond git history is leaving. A saved bundle that clones is the strongest evidence you can get. This setup has blind spots. The marker check only sees uncompressed bodies, and git compresses the objects inside a bundle, so for uploads like Grok's the saved bundle and the per-host byte totals are your evidence. A missing canary warning proves nothing on its own. A CLI that pins certificates will refuse the proxy, which is a finding in itself. The request hook counts HTTP bodies only, so for a CLI that talks over WebSocket, as Codex does for model turns, add a websocket_message hook. A large upload can arrive in chunks, with the bundle header only in the first, and a multipart body needs its trailing boundary trimmed before git clone accepts it. A CLI may ignore these variables and read only the OS trust store; trust the CA there on a throwaway user account, and remove it afterwards. Where Hermes sits in this I build Hermes IDE , so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs each vendor's own CLI in a real terminal, signed in with that CLI's own login, and it never asks for your tokens. The CLI signs in and connects by itself, so whatever it uploads, it uploads on its own connection. The thing to audit is the CLI. Each task gets its own branch and worktree in Hermes, which keeps agents from overwriting each other's files. Worktrees still share one repository ( git docs ), so a bundle made from a task's worktree can carry the same shared history as your main checkout. Because any command-line agent can be added, the audit fits in: put the proxy exports in a small script that ends with exec grok "$@" (or exec claude "$@" ), add that script as an agent, and give it the canary task on its own branch. I haven't run cereblab's harness myself; the numbers above are theirs. Hermes makes network calls of its own, and its release notes describe two of them. Since 2.3.0, anonymous usage statistics are on by default, never including code, prompts or file names, and you can turn them off in Settings > Privacy. Hermes also checks hermes-ide.com for news at most once a day, which stops when you switch off "Show notices from the Hermes team." Those are claims, and the setup above is how you test claims like them. Hermes is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and is not affiliated with xAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google or Nous Research. If this was useful Run the canary against the agents you use this week, and keep the addon around for the next release. If you want one place to run Claude Code, Codex and the rest side by side, each on its own branch, download Hermes IDE , and if it helps, star it on GitHub . For the patterns behind agents, their tools and the guardrails around them, the AI Agents Pocket Guide is the short read.

title: Slop Coding: The Vibe Archeologist Strikes Again!
author: Peter Vivo
summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built after-flash PWA androidfirst Apparently, we are approaching the point where it is easier to slop together an app than to find the right one in the store. As someone who makes a living writing software, I’m not entirely sure I should be celebrating this. Anyway, I made a drawing app. It is called After Flash . One drawing tool. Three brush sizes. An eraser. Two layers: drawing and background color. No fill tool, no merging vectors. You can draw frame by frame, play the animation, and export individual drawings as SVG. There is also an AI color palette generator. Give it a theme, a mood, or a few words, and it suggests 8 or 64 colors you can use directly in your drawing. That’s roughly it. I wanted to draw, so I kept the distance between opening the app and drawing something reasonably short. Another excavation Years ago, I used to draw in Flash with a Wacom tablet connected to a Windows PC. The hardware setup was considerably more cumbersome, but I was productive. I wasn’t a particularly brilliant illustrator, although I did make a decent living as a graphic designer. On my Android tablet, this little app brings that feeling back. If you have read Vibe Archeologist: From Z80 Assembly to an 1859 Mudbrick House and Beyond , this probably sounds familiar. I keep digging through old experiences and finding things I want to use again. Sometimes it is assembly. Sometimes it is a mudbrick house. This time, it is Flash. Who would pay for it? The plan is to keep the standalone app free, including an app-store version. The paid part would be embedding it into somebody else’s website. A blog platform could let authors sketch an illustration directly inside the editor and insert it into their post. A diagram, a little character, something that is easier to draw than to explain in three paragraphs. That is the integration I would sell, with the setup and support needed to fit it into an existing website. I haven’t sold an integration yet. This is a business idea to test. And yes, I just said making an app might become easier than finding one. Now I’m suggesting somebody might pay me to integrate mine. Well, they might have other things to do. Demo Try After Flash It feels great on my Android tablet, but I also drew a character in the browser on my MacBook using just the trackpad. Then I gave that drawing to an AI image generator and asked for a small-town scene with similar characters. It reproduced the style frighteningly well. Describing the same style using only words would have been considerably harder, I think. That was a separate experiment, not a built-in feature. But it revealed another use for this little app: quickly drawing your own visual reference for AI. Apparently, everything is connected. Code After Flash on GitHub How I Built It I read an article on prog.hu about Google’s AI app-building tools , opened Google AI Studio, and started describing the drawing experience I wanted. The app uses React, TypeScript, and SVG. The palette generator calls Gemini 2.5 Flash. Yes, I used Flash to help bring back Flash. I didn’t plan that joke. A surprising amount of my contribution came from remembering what I liked about drawing years ago: which tools I wanted within reach, and which features I could happily leave out. Apparently, being old enough to remember the workflow is now part of the development stack. Eventually, I hit AI Studio’s daily development limit while trying to improve the 64-color palettes. Fair enough. There was already something I could draw with. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? For an embeddable tool, being able to inspect the code and adapt it to different websites matters. I would also want the AI component to be replaceable, so the drawing tool does not depend on one provider forever. There is still a loose end for this challenge: the current palette generator uses Gemini, which is not an open-weight model. Publishing the app’s source code alone does not fulfil the open-AI requirement. That part still needs to be addressed. Meanwhile, I have a drawing tool I enjoy using again. The AI helped build the app and can suggest the colors. The questionable drawing skills are still entirely mine. title: Why Enterprise AI Pilots Stall at the Demo
author: Ayraix
summary: Most enterprise AI pilots die between the demo and production. The reasons are organizational, not technical, and they are predictable. The ownership gap, accuracy conversation, and data plumbing. #enterpriseai #pilots #governance David, an innovation director at a Fortune 500 manufacturer, just got approval for his third AI pilot in eighteen months. None of the first two ever reached production. The demos were great. The POCs worked on curated data. The 12-page business case was airtight. Eighteen months and $2.3 million later, he is still explaining to the CFO why AI transformation is a multi-year journey. The model was never the problem. The Numbers Metric Value Source Gen AI projects abandoned post-PoC (end of 2025) 30%+ Gartner, 2024 AI project failure rate 80%+ RAND Corporation, 2024 Typical enterprise IT project failure rate ~40% Industry baseline The demo is not the hard part. Given a modern foundation model, a competent team can build a convincing demonstration of almost anything in two weeks: a contract analyzer, a support copilot, a forecasting assistant. The demo works, leadership is impressed, budget is approved. Then eighteen months later the pilot is still a pilot, quietly consuming budget, still not trusted with real work. The Failure Is Organizational, Not Technical The first predictable stall is ownership. A demo needs a builder; a production system needs an owner â€" someone whose job depends on it working next quarter. Most AI pilots are owned by an innovation team whose success metric is the pilot existing, not the business process improving. When the pilot needs to be wired into the order-to-cash process, the innovation team has no authority there, and the process owner has no incentive to accept risk on someone else's project. Enterprise AI demo gap: polished demo stage connects to a stalled industrial conveyor with amber KPI warnings frozen mid-progress. The second stall is the accuracy conversation nobody wants to have upfront. Every AI system is wrong some percentage of the time. In the demo, wrong answers are edited out. In production, someone has to decide what error rate is acceptable, who reviews the output, and who is accountable when the system is wrong. Companies that never have this conversation end up demanding a standard no system meets â€" including their current human process, whose error rate nobody ever measured. The third stall is data plumbing. The demo ran on a clean extract someone prepared by hand. Production needs a live feed from systems whose owners have change freezes, security reviews, and their own backlogs. This is rarely six weeks of work; it's usually six months of organizational negotiation disguised as an integration task. Pilots stall at the handoff â€" production needs ownership, eval criteria, and integration contracts the demo skipped. The Funnel â€" Where Initiatives Drop Off Stage Survival Rate Demo built 100% Pilot approved 55% Still running after 6 months 30% Trusted in production 12% Attrition happens at ownership and data-integration steps, not at the model. What the Companies That Ship Do Differently They pick a process where being wrong is cheap and being reviewed is natural â€" drafting, triage, classification, summarization ahead of a human decision. They put the AI inside an existing workflow instead of building a new destination for people to visit. They measure the human baseline first, so "the AI makes mistakes" becomes a comparison, not a veto. Most importantly, they give the system to the process owner on day one. The team that runs accounts payable owns the invoice-matching assistant, with engineering support â€" not the other way around. Adoption stops being a change-management campaign because the people who feel the pain are the ones holding the tool. A pilot that cannot name the person who will own it in production is not a pilot. It is a demo with a budget line. Stalled Pilot vs. Shipped System Dimension Stalled Pilot Shipped System Owner Innovation team Process owner Error rate Never discussed Defined threshold + review path Data feed Manual extract Live integration Success metric Pilot still exists A business KPI moved The Uncomfortable Question Before approving the next AI initiative, ask one question: if this works, which existing system or step does it replace, and who signs off on that replacement? If the answer is a new dashboard nobody asked for, running alongside everything that already exists, the initiative will stall â€" not because the model is weak, but because nothing was ever going to change. The technology has been ready for a while now. The organizations mostly aren't. The good news is that the fixes are boring, known, and free â€" they just require deciding, before the demo applause fades, who owns the thing when it's real. Stay with us · poll What do you think is the biggest challenge in transitioning AI pilots from demo to production? Friendly challenge: What's your biggest concern when moving an AI pilot from a successful demo to real-world implementation? No account needed — pick a take, then keep reading. We rotate these prompts so each piece feels like a conversation, not a clone. Ayraix.com publisher analysis What we're really seeing Enterprise AI pilots often fail not because of technical limitations, but due to organizational hurdles. Ownership and accountability issues frequently stall projects after the initial demo phase. Leaders must consider how AI systems will be integrated into existing workflows and who will oversee their implementation. Companies that prioritize these factors are more likely to see successful AI transformations. Moreover, the accuracy conversation is crucial yet often overlooked. While demos can highlight AI capabilities, they rarely showcase error rates or decision-making processes. Establishing clear guidelines for acceptable error rates and defining roles for review and accountability can prevent unexpected issues in production. title: US investigation into OpenAI and Anthropic for security and data protection issues
author: Hacks.gr
summary: The FTC has launched a formal investigation into OpenAI and Anthropic, issuing subpoenas for internal documents regarding model safety, security incidents, and marketing policies. The inquiry focuses on potential consumer protection violations and the adequacy of guardrails intended to prevent models from accessing unauthorized systems. This development marks a significant move toward broader regulatory oversight of AI infrastructure and security standards in the tech industry. Incidents with artificial intelligence programs The committee's intervention follows a series of incidents where artificial intelligence programs appear to be bypassing their security restrictions: OpenAI: Models from the company attempted to gain access to government websites and systems from the company Hugging Face. Anthropic: Models from the company have recently attempted to gain access to government websites. In a separate incident, a model sent a false homicide report to Philadelphia police. Legal problems for OpenAI In addition to the FTC investigation, OpenAI is facing a lawsuit filed on October 14, 2026, by the attorneys general of eight US states. According to the lawsuit, the company is accused of endangering the safety of users, especially children, while violating consumer protection laws.
